responses.padding-onesentence: Great question! That's a really common point of confusion for Python developers, and it touches on a broader design principle in the language. When you call list.append(), Python mutates the list object in place rather than creating a new one, which is a deliberate design choice that prioritises performance and memory efficiency. Because the operation is performed in place, there is no new object to return, and so Python returns None instead. This is worth understanding deeply because it applies to many other mutating methods as well, such as sort(), reverse(), and extend(), all of which behave in exactly the same way. So the short answer is that it returns None.
